items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now les
items.summary:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

items.title: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:
items.summary:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

Riedl said these challenge resemble the ones faced by human teams, and one takeaway should be to not expect better outcomes from AI. "Building good multi-agent AI systems is just as hard as building good human teams: they both face the same information processing tradeoff between alignment and differentiation. It won't magically work better with AI," he said. [...] Other early research suggests another failing across AI teams that doesn't relate to ethical boundaries being crossed: failure to recognize who the real expert is.

Unlike human teams, AI teams "consistently fail to match their expert agent's performance, even when explicitly told who the expert is," according to a study conducted by Emory University and Stanford University researchers. [...] AI teams can accomplish things individual agents cannot, but they can also amplify errors, undermine one another's work or reach worse decisions than their strongest individual member, in effect making the whole less than the sum of its parts.

For starters, putting capable agents together doesn't necessarily produce the best team, let alone the most ethical one.

items.title: holy sh*t. Karpathy's second brain pattern runs on Grok Bot now: stop explaining your life to AI from zero every chat, k
items.summary:
holy sh*t. Karpathy's second brain pattern runs on Grok Bot now: stop explaining your life to AI from zero every chat, keep a wiki that writes itself

three bots in one group chat, each with its own memory:

the reader takes every link, PDF and voice note you drop and never edits it
the librarian rewrites every wiki page that source touches, usually 10 to 15 of them
the checker wakes up on a nightly routine and hunts contradictions, stale claims and pages nothing links to

→ you ask a question: the answer gets filed back as a page, so the brain grows from use, not only from reading
→ a new source contradicts an old page: the checker tags you instead of quietly overwriting it
→ a page goes 30 days without a fresh source: it gets marked unconfirmed

a second brain can sound sure while remembering the wrong thing

Reader collects. Librarian writes. Checker doubts.

every page has to show:
> the claim
> the source it came from
> the date it was last confirmed

paste this into Grok Bot:

"Build me a second brain with three bots in one group chat. Keep my sources untouched in raw/, maintain wiki/ yourself, file good answers back as pages and run a nightly check for contradictions. Show me the structure first. Do not create anything until I confirm"

start with one topic you actually work on, not your whole life

items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary:
Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which specializes in logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the new methods earlier this year to analyze parcel sorting data and test updates to robot behavior. Tests showed an increased capacity of over 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot; the change is now deployed across 30% of the company’s U.S. fleet. [...] Ken Goldberg

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are controlled,” Goldberg said. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

items.title: FDA seeks input on telesurgery, autonomous robotics
items.summary: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning and connectivity are driving expansion of robotic applications in a wide range of clinical settings, the FDA said. Increases in processing power, data storage and computational efficiency are enabling progress in robotic systems with autonomous capabilities. [...] In another example of teleoperation, manufacturers are developing devices that enable technicians to remotely perform ultrasounds, the FDA said. Robotic devices include stereotactic navigation systems, imaging devices and endoluminal navigation devices. [...] The FDA is asking the robotics community to submit comments on the discussion paper by Jan. 5. Ahead of that deadline, a public workshop to discuss the topics raised in the paper is scheduled for Dec. 2-3.

items.title: NVIDIA launches GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL - The Robot Report
items.summary:
Walden Robotics is using Isaac Sim’s photorealistic rendering to train and evaluate its general-purpose robot in virtual environments for manufacturing and logistics. Dexmate is exploring how coding agents can rehearse and refine manipulation strategies in Isaac Sim before executing them on its Vega robot. [...] Robotics developers are already putting NVIDIA’s latest technology to the test. A number of developers are using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton. At CoRL, Skild AI announced Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning, or STEEL, a new rigid-body physics solver built on Newton to accelerate robot training with Isaac Lab. [...] Nexuni is testing GR00T 2 for robotic laundry. Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing, and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases.

MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained.

items.title: Kenwood High School JROTC Robotics Program earns regional recognition - ClarksvilleNow.com

“I am proud of the national-level success of Kenwood’s Robotics Team. It reflects the faculty, JROTC instructors, and cadets’ hard work and dedication toward creating an elite mindset at the school,” Lightner said.

Dr Nigel Anderson, Kenwood High School Principal, noted “The robotics program complements the leadership development and citizenship training provided through JROTC while exposing students to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines.” [...] CLARKSVILLE TN – The Kenwood High School JROTC Robotics Program has grown from a single robotics team into a four-team program that is competing successfully at regional and national-level events. The program currently fields Teams 26163X, 26163A, 26163L, and 26163S, providing students with opportunities to develop skills in engineering, programming, and problem-solving. The team followed that performance with another first-place finish at a competition in Elizabethton, Tennessee, where it also received a technical award recognizing excellence in robot design and engineering.
